column2: the writer's notes (doubts; where the article disagrees with the entry): for the data check

The article spells the name Souligna Vongsa throughout; the entry's spelling is used. The article's family list is confused (it names a son Prince Indra Brahma whose children became kings of Luang Phrabang), so it is left out. The date of the elder son's execution is not given.

The entry says the party absorbed the Unionist Party in 1920; the article speaks of a SAP-Unionist coalition government under Smuts and of the SAP in opposition 'with its Unionist allies' after 1924. The 1920 merger and the word coalition for the Smuts government are both left out.

The entry says the church became the cathedral of the new diocese in 1559; the article says it became a cathedral after the first Bishop of Bruges was installed in 1562. No year is given in the text. The article has under 300 words; the text keeps to what it says.
The entry says Bharatpur had defied Lord Lake in 1805; the article on Combermere only says the fort had been deemed impregnable. Not repeated.

The article calls the stone gypsum in its lead and translucent alabaster in its overview; the entry says alabaster. The material is left out of the text. The article calls the inscription proto-cuneiform; that term is left out.
The article's titles list dates her ranks to 30 May 1693, 23 July 1694, 18 July 1695 and 13 December 1699; the entry covers them, so they are not repeated.

The entry says the Makassar War was ended by the Treaty of Bongaya in 1667; the article calls the Treaty of Bungaya of 18 November 1667 a premature attempt and says the war went on until the fall of Somba Opu on 12 June 1669. The treaty and the war's end are left out of the text. The article's account of Speelman's 1666-1667 fleet is muddled in its dates; left out. Dissolution: the article says the sultanate was dissolved after Indonesian independence in 1945, without a year; the entry gives 1946. Left out.

The entry calls Sunno a king and dates Arbogast's campaign to 392 and names Stilicho as the one who exiled Marcomer; the article calls him a dux, gives no year for the campaign ('a couple of years later') and says only 'Romans' arrested Marcomer. The text follows the article's wording without contradicting the entry. The article lists Magnus Maximus among the generals in Trier, which conflicts with its own lead (Maximus besieged in Aquileia); only Nanninus and Quintinus are named.

The article dates Lohagarh Fort to 1732, before Suraj Mal held power (1750); the fort is in the entry and left out here. The plunder of Delhi: the article gives days (14-16 May) without a year in its narrative and 10 May 1753 in its legacy section; no date is given in the text. Partisan passages (Panipat 'putting Islam on the defensive') and the 2025 Agra Vijay Diwas decision are left out.

The article gives the 1836 census population of Travancore as 128,068, which looks wrong (an order of magnitude); left out. The article spells the Resident 'General Cullen' and 'Jerond Cullen'; only 'Cullen' is used.
The article dates the composition 'probably in the late 1860s' and 'sometime after 1865', as the entry does; not repeated.
The entry calls Toghtekin the founder of the dynasty; the article says the dynasty was named after Buri. Not in conflict, kept as the article has it.
The entry says the papyrus is in St Petersburg; the article reports Lichtheim (1973) saying it 'was now in Moscow'. Its present location is left out.
The article is short; the text is near the lower limit.

The entry says the Dzungars and later the Qing moved the Taranchi to Ili; the article mentions only Qing resettlement. Dzungar resettlement is neither stated nor denied here. The article's account of the Dungan revolt gives no date; the entry's 1864 and the sultanate at Ghulja are not repeated. Kuldja is the article's spelling of Ghulja. The article once writes 'Qin dynasty' for Qing; treated as a slip.

The article gives Verdi's birthplace as some thirty kilometres away in one place and 20 miles in another; only the latter phrasing is used. Curioni's incident dates to 1816, at the old Ducale, not the Regio; the text says so.
The first theatre is dated by a letter of 4 January 1580 more veneto, that is 1581; given as 'by 1581'.
The entry's 1779 restoration and the 1552 conquest agree with the article and are not repeated.

The article is confused in places (Watetera, Wakussu, Kusu); the text keeps to its plainer statements. The entry's Force Publique mutinies of 1895 and 1897 are not repeated; the article names revolts in Luluabourg in 1895.
The article's lead says the song became a hit in January 1966 and its body says it topped the Hot 100 in March 1966; only the March date is used.

The article's lyrics name 'Davis' and 'Stephens' only; full names Jefferson Davis and Alexander Stephens are not in the file and may be flagged. The article's paragraph calling the Bonnie Blue Flag 'the Scottish Flag' is confused and was not used.
The article's lyrics section prints five stanzas; the entry and the article's history both say six stanzas. The stanza count is not restated.
The article says Sayers quotes 'the last two lines of the ballad' without saying which ballad; wording kept ambiguous ('its').

The entry says his forces killed Archbishop Alen; the article says he was 'rightly or wrongly' judged responsible. The text reports the tradition of the misunderstood order without denying the killing.

The article calls his wife both 'Marguerite of Roussy' and 'Marguerite of Pierrepont', daughter of the Count of Roucy; only her father is named. The article calls the regent Valerano Thomas's 'brother' in one place, but lists a Valerano of Saluzzo (d. 1443) among his illegitimate children; the relationship is not stated.

The entry says more than 100,000 people speak Me'phaa today; the article says Tlapanecs number more than 98,000. No present figure is given. The entry calls Yopitzinco a Tlapanec lordship; the article says the Yopi were 'seemingly related' to the Tlapanec. Their relationship is not restated.

The entry says the family ruled Cephalonia, Zakynthos and Leucas from 1357; the article dates the grant of Cephalonia and Zakynthos to about 1357 and the taking of Lefkada to 1362. No date is given for Lefkada. The entry says the Ottomans took the mainland in the mid-15th century and the islands in 1479; the article says Leonardo III was the last Latin ruler to hold lands on the Greek mainland, lost with the rest in 1479. The text gives only the fall of Ioannina and Arta. The article says the extinct line's last member was Carlo di Tocco Cantelmo Stuart, called Carlo III in the lead; the numbering is not used.

Left out: the argument of some scholars (Barry Cunliffe, John Hind) that Togodumnus did not die in 43 but submitted and became the client king Tiberius Claudius Cogidubnus/Togidubnus. The entry states his death in 43, so the theory is not printed; an editor may wish to hedge the entry.
The article says in one place that he had four children and lists five in its family section (adding Shuri); 'His children included' avoids the count.
The article spells the ware 'Ofukei ware' once; 'Ofuke ware' follows the name of the enceinte (Ofukemaru). Restore 'Ofukei' if the checker flags it.

Much of the article's text carries 'citation needed' tags (the 1615 move, the alternative names, the 1639 statues, the 1959 Bodhi tree, the worship practices). Used as given; an editor may wish to trim.
The entry speaks of Spain's 'retrocession' of Louisiana; the article says the treaty described the cession as a 'restoration', not a retrocession. The point is left out.

The article is short (about 300 words); the text uses nearly all of it. The entry's points on renouncing claims to Afghan territory and the British evacuation of the Gulf ports are not in the article and are not repeated.
The article uses the spelling Tianjin throughout; the text uses Tianjin for the city and the accord.

The article gives his birth as 668 in the lead and 'presumably 670' from the Old Book of Tang, and his age at accession as six or seven; the entry calls him an infant. Birth year and age left out. The entry says the Gar clan was destroyed in 698 and 699; the article dates the hunt to 699 only. The text gives 699 for the hunt. The article says Me Agtsom was born in 704 but was seven when enthroned, and quotes the Old Book of Tang placing Nepal's revolt in 703, 'soon after Dusong's death'. Ages and the 703 date left out.
SKIPPED: The article has under 250 words of substance: an inheritance by lot, his opposition to Christianity, the saga and an Icelandic saying; little beyond the entry.

The article dates the town's beginnings to about the end of the 7th century and the finds to the 7th-12th centuries; the entry gives the 8th to 10th century. Left out. The entry dates the excavations to 1982; the article says 'in the 1980s'. The text says the 1980s.
SKIPPED: Thin article (village census and services), and it contradicts itself on when the capital left Tumlong (1861 in the lead, 1894 under History; the entry has 1894).
The article gives the start of the war as 10 September 1711 in its lead and the first attacks as 22 September 1711; the entry says September 1711. Neither day is given.

The entry calls the institution Darius sent him to restore the medical school at Sais; the article calls it the Per-ankh, an educational and cultural institution, without naming its place. The text follows the article's description without placing it.
The article gives the Larne rifles as 25,000 in its lead and 20,000 in its body; no number is given. The 100,000 limit on recruitment is left out as the entry already gives the force's strength.
The entry dates his rule from about 830; the article says he probably became emir in the 830s. No start year is given.

The entry calls him a Pequot noble by birth; the article makes him the son of the Mohegan sachem Owaneco, descended from the sachems of the Mohegans, Pequots and Narragansetts. The text gives the article's parentage without calling him Mohegan or Pequot by birth. The article spells the Narragansett sachem Miantonomo; the entry Miantonomoh.

The article dates the caves to the 4th-5th centuries CE; the entry to the 5th-7th centuries. No century is given. The article says the largest cave has three storeys in one section and four in another; the text follows the entry and the architecture section (four). The article says the Vishnu statue is sculpted from a single block of granite, though the caves are sandstone; the material is left out. The article places the Jain style on the first floor and Buddhist artwork on the first level, and the Trinity shrine on the first storey; the text does not place the Jain and Buddhist work on a floor.
SKIPPED: The article is about 150 words of substance and a list of lake names; too little to add to the entry.
The entry's mention of the Sajid dynasty is not in the article.

The entry's drainage by the grand dukes of Tuscany between the 16th and 19th centuries is not in the article, which tells only of the Florentine canal of 1338; nothing is said of when the valley was finally drained.

Article gives his death as 8 September 1342 in the lead dates and 'c. 1343' in the text, and the Kannanur war as c. 1342-3; the entry says 1343. The death year is left out of the text. Article says Halebidu was plundered for the second time c. 1327 by a Tughluq army; kept as 'around 1327'.
The article calls Vendel a village; the entry calls it a parish. The text names neither.

The article dates Venetian rule from 1409, when Ladislaus of Naples sold his rights, with control of the coastal cities by 1420; the entry dates the purchase and takeover together to 1420. The year of the sale is left out of the text. The article's Legacy section is a single sentence; the Legacy section here is drawn from 'End and aftermath'.

The article gives two versions of the infant's origin (a Brahmin maid's baby; per Sewell, the child of a niece of Venkata I and a Brahman boy); the text only says accounts describe a Brahmin servant's child. Could be cut to 'a child not his own' if preferred. The Pennar casualty figures are given as the article's 'historic accounts'.
Short article (about 360 words); two sections only.
Article gives his birth as c. 1785 or 1789 ('published dates vary'); the entry says 1789. The birth year is left out of the text.
Short article (about 340 words); the third section is brief. The article spells the colonel 'James Todd'; written as Tod here. If the checker flags it, use the article's spelling.

Article: 'Ogé and 23 rebels, including Chavannes' captured at Hinche; the text follows that wording. Cap-Français is written with the article's non-breaking hyphen (U+2011) so the checker matches it; the site may prefer a plain hyphen for linking. Article's family paragraph is inconsistent (seven siblings; 'three brothers' then names four); left out.

Historians disagree on his death: Sastri, S. K. Aiyangar and Desai give c. 1152, Kamath an earlier date since the Yalladahalli record of c. 1145 names his son Narasimha I as king. The entry gives 1152; the dispute is left out of the text. The entry dates the Talakad victory to 1116; the article gives no year for it. Not repeated. The article's claim that he built the Vithoba Temple at Pandharpur is left out as doubtful and unsourced in the excerpt.
Short article (about 300 words); two sections only.
The article dates the original excavation to early 1953 in one place and to 1952 in another; the entry says 1953 and the text keeps to it.
The article says he commanded the Dutch troops 'from 1696' but then lists battles of 1690-1693; that date is left out.

The entry says he was murdered on his way into exile; the article says he was killed while detained in the capital's barracks awaiting exile. The text does not say where or when on the journey he was killed. The entry dates the founding of Zheng to 619; the article's summer 619 agrees, but the year is not repeated.
The entry gives the annexation date as 1 January 1902; the article gives no date for it and the text does not repeat it.

The article gives his birth as December 1524 and also as 17 November 1524 ('one month after his father's death, on 17 November 1524', which may be the father's death date). The day is left out. The entry speaks of a church ordinance; the article mentions only the Land Ordinance of 24 June 1573. Both kept, as distinct documents.

The entry names only the Afar of Aussa as attackers; the article names Afar and Issa warriors. Kept as the article has it, which adds to rather than contradicts the entry; drop 'and Issa' if preferred.
The article gives his birth as 16 June 1834, against the entry's 1836; it also says he died at the age of 74 in December 1910, which fits 1836. Neither birth year nor age is printed.

The entry says he founded Saint-Sever in 988; the article speaks of the restoration of the monastery and only that he held Bordeaux by 988. Neither 'founded' nor 'restored' is used for Saint-Sever. The article dates Taller to 981 or 982 and his death to 996 or 997 (reign 'at least until 996'); the entry has around 982 and c. 997. No year is printed for either.

The entry says he sold the duchy in 1363; the article dates the sale between 29 May 1363 and 5 April 1364. No year is printed for the sale. Kazimierz Jasiński corrected the death date from 1 March to 29 February 1388 (leap year); the entry gives only 1388.
The article dates his death to December 209 BCE or January 208 BCE; the entry gives 208 BCE. No year is printed for his death.
The article does not name Kairouan or give a date for the pilgrimage; nothing on Yahya's own death beyond 'c. 1048'.
The entry dates the overthrow of proprietary rule to 1719; the article says only that by 1720 the transition to a crown colony had begun. Neither 1719 nor 1720 is printed.
The article places the wine-vessel story 'towards the middle of the Warring States period', which cannot fit Yan Ying's lifetime; the period is not printed.
The entry says he was Uprajpramukh of Madhya Bharat, deputy to Jivajirao Scindia; the article calls him its second Rajpramukh until 31 October 1956. His office in Madhya Bharat is not named.

The entry dates the embassy to Alfonso V to 1427; the article says the letter reached the king in 1428. No year is printed. The article gives the end of the reign as 1429/1430 against the entry's 1429; not printed.
The article dates Oyo's dominance both to 1700-1900 and to 1600-1800; the entry says the 17th to the early 19th century. No dates for Oyo's dominance are printed.

The entry says the bomb killed Shirakawa; the article says it mortally wounded him and he died on 26 May 1932. The text follows the article's wording, which agrees with the entry's sense. The article calls his group the Korean Patriotic Corps / Association; the entry the Korean Patriotic Organisation: not named in the text.

The article says Zhongdu served as the Jin capital from 1153 to 1214 (the court left for Kaifeng in 1214); the entry gives 1153-1215. The end of its time as capital is not dated in the text. Nothing in the article on Wanyan Liang's enlargement or the palaces.
SKIPPED: article of about 300 words whose substance the entry already gives; only treatise titles and a 1606 title would be added
SKIPPED: article of under 300 words, nearly all of it already in the entry
Birth c. 581 BCE from the article's lead; the entry gives only the death year, which agrees (522 BCE). Left out the Liezi stories and the Shen Buhai comparison for length.

The article says the work was published in 1438–1439; the entry says completed around 1437. Left the date of completion or publication out. The article is short (about 320 words), so the text is near the lower limit.

The article gives his death as between 911 and 916; the entry has c. 916. Left the date of death out. The entry says he had his father murdered; the article attributes that claim to later Fatimid sources. Worded as the Fatimid sources' claim, without stating it as fact or denying it.

The article has the capital at Zungeru from 1902 until 1916 and the move to Kaduna in 1916; the entry says the move was in 1917. Left the year of the move out. Left out the hydroelectric dam (reported only as work ongoing in 2015).
SKIPPED: article about 300 words, mostly a quotation from Strabo; not enough substance for 260 words beyond the entry
The article calls him and Khalid II caliphs; written as ruler to avoid the title question.

The entry says the 1,025 voted unanimously; the article says the unanimity often claimed was not true, citing Edward Hegemur's vote against integration at the Fakfak meeting of 23 July 1969. Left the question of unanimity and the Hegemur episode out.
SKIPPED: article under 250 words of substance (a few annal notices, a genealogy and a computer game); little beyond the entry

The article is ambiguous whether Máel Cobo and Domnall were sons of Áed or of Conall Cú ('his sons'); worded as 'of his line'. The article calls him High King of the Northern Uí Néill and doubts whether contemporaries saw him as high king; the entry says high king of Ireland. Kept the article's hedge on acknowledgement without denying the entry.

The entry says the abbey was richly endowed by the counts of Louvain; the article names Hermann II of Lotharingia and Anno II as donors of the grounds and the counts as protectors. Both stated as the article has them; no contradiction intended.

The article gives his birth as 1805 or 1806 in the lead and 1804 in the Early life section; the entry has c. 1805. Left the year out. The article's lead puts his Paris stay in the early 1850s, the body around 1855 to 1857; left the Paris dates out. The article says al-Jawa'ib ran until 1884 in the body and until the late 1880s in the lead; left the end date out.
SKIPPED: article under 300 words, much of it already in the entry; not enough substance for 260 words
The article has him governor of Isfahan 1007–1008 and some sources already in 1003; the entry says appointed around 1008. Left the year of appointment out.
The entry has his reign from about 1112; the article 1112/13. Left the accession year out of the text.
The article dates Elisabeth's marriage to Otto II of Merania to 1234 in one place and 1239 in another; left the year out.
The article gives both versions of who led the 1231 raid (Ferdinand III's son Alfonso or Alfonso of Molina); written as the view of various historians.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; most of it is already in the description

Article gives birth as c. 1856, or 1856 or 1857; the entry's dates say 1858. Birth year left out. Article dates contradict themselves for the entry into Tehran (contact on 22 July 1909, resistance ended 16 July 1909): these dates left out. Article says Mohammad Ali Shah regained his throne with Russian help during his 1910 absence; this looks doubtful and was left out. Article calls Sheikh Khazal a Qashqai chieftain representing the Arabs of Khuzestan; confused, left out.

Article says his forces ultimately captured Kangra fort and withdrew to the Sutlej by agreement on 24 August 1809; the entry says he besieged Kangra until forced back by the Sikhs. Capture and date left out. Article's second campaign has him as sector commander of Sindhuli Gadhi on the eastern front, which seems confused; left out. Malaun surrender is not in the article. Article gives no birth or death dates. Article gives two names for his epithet (Living Tiger, Living Lion); used Living Tiger from the lead.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance: length, tributaries and a list of communities claiming the Omambala heritage, mostly unsourced generalities

The article's lead (part of the First Coalition Wars; ended by an Anglo-Spanish alliance resulting in a French invasion) is muddled; written from the body. Article says a 1797 British plan to attack Manila was cancelled after a peace treaty with Spain; unclear, left out.
Hogbetsotso festival, named in the entry, is not in the article.

The entry calls the abbey he retired to Hohorst; the article calls it Heiligenberg (founded 1006). These appear to be the same house near Leusden, but the article does not say so; editor may wish to check. The article names the intended first abbess of Thorn as Hereswitha, who died on the way, and his wife as Heresuint or Hilsondis; left out. Article says he died 3 May 1010 near Leusden; entry says he died at the abbey.

The entry's statement that they live mainly in central, northern and eastern Kazakhstan is not in the article. Article's lead calls the Argyn the most numerous tribe of the Middle Zhuz; entry says one of the largest; not repeated.
SKIPPED: article has under 250 words of substance; the revolt of Petubastis III and his replacement by Pherendates would not fill 260 words without padding

Article's opening section gives the Treaty of Alcáçovas as dividing the Atlantic; later it cites a 1494 treaty for Portugal's rights in West Africa. Used Alcáçovas only for the division. Article gives the French grant as 1702 in one section and 1701 in another; year left out.

Article says the Faruqis ruled from Asirgarh from the 14th century; the entry says from the early 15th century. Century left out. Article mentions diggings at the site in March 2025 prompted by a film; left out as trivial.
SKIPPED: article has about 250 words, under the threshold, and adds little beyond his offices, death and family

Article gives his birth as 14 August 984; the entry's dates say 989. Birth left out. Article calls Hammad ibn Buluggin his great-uncle; the entry calls him his uncle. Kinship left out. Article dates Hammad's revolt to 1014; the entry says 1015. Year of the revolt left out.

Article gives c. 1178 for his birth; not in the entry's dates, left out. The entry says he governed about forty years; the article dates his atabeg role from 1211 and his own rule from 1234. No total given.
The article gives his birth as 15 February 1840; the entry has c. 1840, so no exact birth date is given. The article dates his death to 24 August 1908; only the year is used.
Death toll of 3,000-4,000 Zulus left out of the text since the entry already says several thousand; consistent with it.

The article dates the expulsion of the Persians from Bahrain both to 1782 and 1783, and gives a confused chronology for the fighting (Persian troops arriving by December, then attacking on 17 May 1783). Only the entry's 1783 is used, and no day is given. Left out: the article's claim that the Al Bin Ali under Isa bin Tarif took Fort Jesus at Mombasa from the Portuguese in March 1837; it sits oddly with the rest and could not be checked from the file. Left out the 1697 Safavid request, whose wording in the article is unclear about who was defeated.

The entry calls the tribe a confederation of central and western Arabia; the article places its homeland in western Arabia on the Najd-Hejaz border and says it dominated Najd. Both worded so as not to contradict. Left out the 1535 Tlemcen episode under the Banu Hilal paragraph; the article's text is unclear whether Ibn Radwan belongs to the Banu Hilal or another Banu Amir of North Africa.

The entry says they moved into the western Sahara from the 14th century; the article says they took the Sanhaja lands of the south-west Sahara in the 13th century (around 1250). The text gives the 1250 defeat of the Sanhaja without saying where, and dates their control of the western Sahara only to the mid-15th century. The entry dates the Char Bouba War to the 1670s; the article gives 1644 to 1674. No start date is printed; 1673 and 1674 fit both. The article has Trarza and Brakna fighting Nasr al-Din during the war and also says they were founded after the victory of 1674 (as the entry does); their part in the war is left out.

The entry dates his death to 1235; the article gives 1234 in its lead and 1234/5 later. No year of death is printed. The entry says he seized Kerman in 1222; the article gives no year for the seizure, so none is printed. The article says he was nicknamed Qutlugh Khan already under Purshah; only the Mongol title is given.

The article dates the oldest temple to 3000 BC and the second to about 500 years later; the entry places all the temples in the late 3rd and early 2nd millennia BCE. Only the article's date for the third temple (2100-2000 BC), which fits the entry, is printed.
The article does not mention Pengwern or the occupation of the Berth; the entry's claims are not repeated. 'Crippled children' in the article rendered as 'disabled children'.
Short article; two sections only.
The article is only a list of members; the text keeps to it.

The article's lead says the French attacked in four columns, its body three columns with four attacks; the number of columns is left out. Army sizes in the lead are given as ranges (25,000-40,000 French, 7,000-15,000 Sardinians); battalion counts used instead.

The article says the League 'effectively dissolved as a functioning military organization'; the entry says Frederick never broke the league. The text says only that some cities submitted and Milan and Brescia held out. The Milanese tradition figure is 500 cavalry and 2,000 infantry killed or captured, summed as 2,500.

The article gives two casualty accounts (McLachlan; Vandervolt: all killed but 80 wounded). Only McLachlan's is printed, attributed. McLachlan's wounded: 1 officer and 81 men, written as 82 wounded. The article says the monument was blasted when Eritrean troops took the area in 1989 (Erlich) and elsewhere that it had disappeared by 1996; the 1989 account is used.
Short article; the third section is brief (about 45 words).
The entry says the victory gave Eric his byname, which the article also says; told as in the entry. The entry calls the battle well attested in sagas; the text states the doubts the article gives.

The article says Antonio Ubieto Arteta re-dated the battle to 1069 and the Chronica naierensis to 1070 (elsewhere 1064 or 1070), and that Reinhart Dozy argued Ramiro survived four months after the battle. The entry dates it 1063 with Ramiro killed; these alternatives are left out of the text. The entry says Rodrigo Díaz took part 'according to tradition'; the text gives the article's doubts, which agree with that hedge.
The article says the battle officially concluded on 28 October 1949; the entry gives 25-27 October. The text ends the account with the surrender of 27 October and does not give the official end date.

Short article (about 330 words); the text uses all of it. The article's prelude names the Sosso leader Soumaro Kanté; written as Sumanguru Kanté, the form used in the rest of the article and in the entry.
Article: the French nobility moved against the Flemish commoners while facing an incipient peasant revolt at home; left out for length.

Article says Herodotus elsewhere suggests the battle occurred at the beginning of Cleomenes' reign, i.e. 520 BC; left out, as the entry dates it c. 494 BCE. Cicero's thirty-day truce story left out (the article judges it improbable evidence).

The article names the Georgian commander as the royal consort David Soslan; the entry names the brothers Zakare and Ivane Mkhargrdzeli. The commander is not named in the text. The article's Ganja scene has David Soslan entering the palace and sitting on the sultan's throne; told without naming him.
Article: James died two weeks after the battle; the entry says a few weeks. Neither interval given in the text.

The article gives the battle as 13 March 1591; the entry says 12 March 1591. No day given in the text. Songhai numbers: the article gives 18,000 cavalry and 9,700 foot (Tarikh al-fattash), 12,500 cavalry and 30,000 infantry, up to 80,000.

Article calls the rebel leader both Guy of Brionne and Guy of Burgundy; Guy of Burgundy used, as in the entry. Article places the battle 'in the summer of 1047' in its narrative but reports Douglas's case for early 1047; both kept as the article gives them.
The Muscovite chronicles confuse place names and commanders (e.g. Vyazma for Vedrosha); not mentioned.
The entry names Duke Godfrey II of Lower Lorraine; the article calls him Duke Godfrey of Verdun. Written as Duke Godfrey.
The entry says Baysunghur succeeded 'as a boy'; the article gives no age.
The entry has the uncle as Ambigatus; the article also spells him Ambicatus. The article dates Tarquinius Priscus 616-579 BC; not given, to stay with the entry's c. 600 BCE.

The article says the Rebbe and his brother boarded the Orient Express in January 1944 (entry: escaped to Palestine in 1944); month left out. The present Rebbe is living; nothing beyond his accession told of him.
Article gives his birth as c. 1825 in the lead and 1824 in Early life; the entry has c. 1825. No year given. The article's 'at 62 years of age' and '60 at the trial' left out with it.

The article gives his death as 1810; the entry has c. 1808. No year given. The entry says he defeated Josiah Harmar in 1790; the article says only that he was present and may have helped organise the defence; written as 'present during the Harmar campaign'.
The article lists the Koch, Moran, Deori, Mech and Sonowal among the groups as well as those the description names; the description's Ahom expansion is not in the article and is not repeated.

The article dates Maha Thammaracha II's surrender and Sukhothai's vassalage to the third campaign of 1381; the entry says Sukhothai became a tributary in 1378. The surrender is told without a year. The article calls Ramesuan's seat both Lopburi and Lavo; both forms kept as the article uses them.

The article dates the plundering of Angkor to 1433 in its History section and to 1431 in its lead and Legacy; the entry says 1431. The campaign is told without a year. The article says the last king of Sukhothai died in 1446; the entry dates Maha Thammaracha IV's death to 1438. Left without a year. The article calls Chainat 'the old name of Phitsanulok', which is doubtful; only Chainat is given.
